content: 1. Shattuck and Johnson, along with their colleagues, conducted a study examining changes in sexual risk behaviors among participants enrolled in a clinical trial for HIV prevention using pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The findings were published in the journal Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2008. 2. Wilton, Senn, Sharma, and Tan reviewed the role of PrEP in managing sexually acquired HIV risk. Their comprehensive review, published in HIV AIDS (Auckland) in 2015, highlighted the effectiveness and challenges of PrEP implementation. 3. Young and McDaid conducted a review of research on the acceptability of oral PrEP and its use as a preventive treatment. Their findings, published in AIDS and Behavior in 2014, explored factors influencing the adoption of PrEP among various populations. 4. UNAIDS organized a consultation meeting in Johannesburg in November 2013 to gather insights from sex workers regarding their hopes and concerns about PrEP. The recommendations from this meeting were documented by the Wits Reproductive Health and HIV Institute. 5. The International Network of People Who Use Drugs published a report in 2014 discussing harm reduction strategies, hepatitis C management, and perspectives on PrEP from the drug-using community. 6. Nwagwu, Georges, and Weathers explored perceived barriers to adopting PrEP among male-to-female transgender youth. Their findings were presented in the Communicating Nursing Research journal in 2013. 7. Van der Straten, Stadler, Montgomery, and colleagues conducted a qualitative study on women’s experiences with oral and vaginal PrEP in Johannesburg, South Africa. This study, part of the VOICE-C trial, was published in PLOS One in 2014. 8. Bekker, Hughes, Amico, and Grant, as part of the HPTN 067/ADAPT Cape Town study, compared daily and non-daily PrEP dosing regimens among African women. Their findings were presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle in February 2015. 9. UNITAID published the second edition of its report on the HIV prevention technology and market landscape in November 2014, providing an overview of advancements and challenges in the field. 10. Gomez, Borquez, Case, Wheelock, and Vassall conducted a systematic review of cost-effectiveness modeling studies on scaling up PrEP for HIV prevention. Their findings, published in PLOS Medicine in 2013, assessed the financial and public health impact of PrEP implementation. 11. Alistar, Owens, and Brandeau evaluated the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of oral PrEP as part of a portfolio of prevention programs for injection drug users in mixed HIV epidemics. Their study was published in PLOS One in 2014. 12. Grant, Lama, Goicochea, Levy, and Marseille performed a cost-effectiveness analysis of HIV chemoprophylaxis, presenting their findings at the World AIDS Conference in Toronto in 2006. 13. The Clinton Health Access Initiative released a 2014 antiretroviral (ARV) ceiling price list, providing critical information on the affordability of ARV drugs. 14. Rosengarten and Michael examined the role of expectations in translating treatment into prevention, focusing on the case of HIV PrEP. Their analysis was published in Social Science & Medicine in 2009. 15. A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted to inform the 2015 WHO guidelines on antiretroviral therapy (ART). The review aimed to update evidence on the optimal timing for initiating ART, focusing on clinical outcomes such as mortality, severe HIV disease, malignancy, AIDS-related events, non-AIDS events, tuberculosis, and treatment-related adverse events. 16. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cohort studies comparing outcomes in patients initiating ART at higher CD4 counts (≥500 cells/μL) versus lower CD4 counts (200–499 cells/μL). The evidence was graded for quality, with moderate evidence supporting earlier ART initiation to reduce disease progression and HIV transmission, and low evidence for its association with severe adverse events. 17. The search strategy for the review spanned multiple databases, including PubMed, CENTRAL, SCOPUS, and the WHO Global Index Medicus, covering studies published between 1996 and 2015. The inclusion criteria focused on studies comparing clinical and laboratory outcomes in patients initiating ART at different CD4 thresholds. 18. The review identified 20 studies, including 10 new studies and 10 from a previous review. Data were synthesized from single cohorts and large pooled cohorts, predominantly from North America and Europe, involving tens of thousands of participants. 19. Mortality outcomes were reported in one RCT and six observational studies. The quality of evidence from the RCT was low due to imprecision, while the observational studies had very low quality due to overlapping patient populations and indirect comparisons. 20. Evidence on HIV disease progression suggested a lower risk of severe infections with earlier ART initiation. However, the quality of evidence was downgraded due to imprecision and lack of adjustment for confounders in some studies. 21. The findings from this review will inform the 2015 WHO guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for HIV treatment and prevention, emphasizing the benefits of earlier ART initiation while acknowledging the limitations of the available evidence.
